clue.text: Some remarkable Norfolk talent discovered in traditional story

indicators.note: something discovered in the words is found sitting within them, so the answer is a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: A gifted East Anglian turns up in an old yarn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some remarkable' only dresses the surface; the answer runs across 'NorFOLK TALEnt'. Norfolk is an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: A folk tale is a story handed down orally among ordinary people, a classic traditional narrative.

clue.text: Is Kosinski's polo player a cautious socialist?

definitions.meaning: Jerzy Kosinski's novel Passion Play has a polo-playing hero
a member of Britain's ... Society, which favoured gradual, step-by-step reform

explanation.surface: A question whether a novelist's sporting hero holds careful left-wing views.
explanation.definitionFit: The Fabian Society took its name from a Roman general famed for delaying tactics, hence gradualist socialism; Kosinski's sporting protagonist bears the same name.

clue.text: Dramatically associated with Richardson heroine by Isaac Bickerstaffe

definitions.text: Dramatically associated with Richardson heroine by Isaac Bickerstaffe

parts.words: Dramatically associated with Richardson heroine by Isaac Bickerstaffe
parts.note: Bickerstaffe's comic opera pairs a hero's name with Clarissa, the heroine of Samuel Richardson's novel, in its title

explanation.surface: A literary question about which character an eighteenth-century dramatist paired with a novelist's heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Bickerstaffe's 1768 comic opera is titled with this hero's name followed by 'and Clarissa', Richardson's best-known heroine.

clue.text: Old man of the Scandinavian Theatre

definitions.text: Old man of the Scandinavian Theatre

parts.words: Old man of the Scandinavian Theatre
parts.note: 'old man' is slang for a dad, and Strindberg's Swedish tragedy of 1887 carries that paternal title

explanation.surface: A veteran figure of Nordic drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Strindberg's play about a captain driven mad by doubt over his paternity is a landmark of Scandinavian drama; 'old man' is informal for a parent.

clue.text: Surely the epitome of prejudice and pride?

definitions.text: Surely the epitome of prejudice and pride?

parts.words: Surely the epitome of prejudice and pride?
parts.note: the reversed title of Jane Austen's novel points to its haughtiest character, Darcy's snobbish aunt

explanation.surface: A rhetorical question about who best embodies two classic vices.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue swaps Austen's title round so it reads as a plain description of a person.
explanation.definitionFit: In Austen's novel Darcy's aunt, Lady Catherine, is the snob par excellence, scorning Elizabeth Bennet's lowly connections.

clue.text: To bark uncontrollably for composer

indicators.note: acting uncontrollably suggests the letters running wild into a new order

explanation.surface: A dog barking out of control in honour of a musician.
explanation.definitionFit: Béla Bartók was a Hungarian twentieth-century composer.

clue.text: "… regards that stand / — from the entire point" (King Lear)

definitions.text: "… regards that stand / — from the entire point" (King Lear)

parts.words: "… regards that stand / — from the entire point" (King Lear)
parts.note: the gap in France's line about love mixed with irrelevant considerations is filled by a word meaning apart or distant

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's tragedy with one word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: In King Lear, France says love is not love when mingled with regards that stand apart, distant from the main point.

clue.text: Area of Macbeth's Scotland in which the nomad went astray

indicators.note: a wanderer who went astray has lost his way, so the letters lose their order

explanation.surface: A wandering traveller gets lost in Macbeth's part of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth is Thane of Glamis and Cawdor; a thane's domain or territory is his jurisdiction.

clue.text: London district in Canada

parts.note: the novelist Jack London set much of his fiction in a Yukon gold-rush region, not a part of the English capital

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood of the British capital somehow sited across the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'London' looks like the city; it is Jack London, whose gold-rush stories made this Yukon region his territory.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yukon gold-rush region of the 1890s is the setting of Jack London's stories such as The Call of the Wild.

clue.text: They are the last word, offering support to authors

definitions.text: They are the last word, offering support to authors

parts.words: They are the last word, offering support to authors
parts.note: the final pages of a volume, or the props that keep writers' volumes upright on a shelf

explanation.surface: Praise for people who are definitive and help writers.
explanation.definitionFit: Supports placed at each end of a row of volumes hold them upright; read literally the phrase also means a volume's closing pages.

clue.text: Eaten by some of Van Gogh's subjects

definitions.text: Eaten by some of Van Gogh's subjects

parts.words: Eaten by some of Van Gogh's subjects
parts.note: Van Gogh's 1885 painting shows a peasant family at supper on a starchy tuber

explanation.surface: A note on what the people in Van Gogh's paintings ate.
explanation.definitionFit: Van Gogh's dark early masterpiece The Potato Eaters shows Dutch peasants sharing their humble meal.

clue.text: "Everybody said she was the most — -looking child ever seen" (Frances Hodgson-Burnett)

definitions.text: "Everybody said she was the most — -looking child ever seen" (Frances Hodgson-Burnett)

parts.words: "Everybody said she was the most — -looking child ever seen" (Frances Hodgson-Burnett)
parts.note: the opening of The Secret Garden describes sour, unpleasant Mary Lennox, and the gap takes a word meaning unpleasant

explanation.surface: A quotation from a children's classic with a word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: The Secret Garden opens by calling Mary Lennox the most sour, unpleasant-looking child anyone had seen.

clue.text: Venue associated with sangre by Ibafiez ()

definitions.text: Venue associated with sangre by Ibafiez

parts.words: Venue associated with sangre by Ibafiez
parts.note: Blasco Ibáñez's bullfighting novel pairs blood with the sandy ring of the bullring in its title

explanation.surface: Which venue a Spanish novelist linked with blood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ibafiez' is the OCR of Ibáñez. Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's novel is 'Sangre y arena', Blood and Sand.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish word for sand also names a bullring, the setting of Blasco Ibáñez's matador novel.

clue.text: Hardy specimen produced by W. S. Maugham

definitions.text: Hardy specimen produced by W. S. Maugham

parts.words: Hardy specimen produced by W. S. Maugham
parts.note: Maugham's novel Cakes and Ale features a grand old novelist widely taken to be modelled on Thomas Hardy

explanation.surface: A tough plant grown by a famous author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like robust; it is Thomas Hardy, of whom Maugham's Edward Driffield in Cakes and Ale was thought a portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Driffield, the venerable novelist in Cakes and Ale, was read as a sketch of Thomas Hardy.

clue.text: Durrell's Festival of Paris

parts.note: Lawrence Durrell's early novel, written in Paris and published there by Obelisk Press, carries a dark title

explanation.surface: A celebration in the French capital put on by a novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence Durrell's 1938 novel was first published in Paris by Jack Kahane's Obelisk Press.

clue.text: Austrian money for French composers

definitions.meaning: small copper and silver coins once current in Austria and South Germany
Rodolphe Kreutzer, the French violinist-composer to whom Beethoven dedicated a sonata, taken in the plural

explanation.surface: Viennese cash paid to Parisian musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: The kreuzer was an old Austrian coin; Rodolphe Kreutzer was a French composer and violinist, here pluralised.

clue.text: Artistic rubbing (French) — over the top but on time

parts.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: An excessive but punctual French art technique.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis and dash only dress the surface; 'but on' links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The technique of taking a rubbing from a textured surface with pencil or crayon, used by Max Ernst.

clue.text: Vita size wrongly reported in Russian publication

indicators.note: letters placed wrongly are in the wrong order, so they must be put right

explanation.surface: A report gets the measurements of something wrong in a Moscow paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reported' looks like a sound-alike signal but just completes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet government's daily newspaper, its title meaning 'news'.

clue.text: A sharp chamber piece by Haydn?

definitions.text: A sharp chamber piece by Haydn?

parts.words: A sharp chamber piece by Haydn?
parts.note: a work for four strings nicknamed after a keen-edged shaving tool, said to have been bartered by Haydn for a good blade

explanation.surface: Asking whether a keen piece of chamber music is by Haydn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A sharp' looks like a musical key; the nickname comes from Haydn reportedly trading the piece for a good shaving blade.
explanation.definitionFit: Haydn's String Quartet Op. 55 No. 2 is nicknamed for a shaving implement he reputedly received for it.

clue.text: Miss Christie in saga that never ends

indicators.note: a saga that never ends has lost its beginning and close, so drop the first and last letters

parts.note: not a hidden word placed by the setter as such, a coincidence of the method: removing the outer letters of this run naturally leaves its inner letters in a row

explanation.surface: A crime writer caught in an endless family story.
explanation.walkthrough: Take 'saga that' as one string and lose its first and last letters; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha is the first name of the crime novelist Christie.

clue.text: Some papers of James (according to North)

definitions.text: Some papers of James (according to North)

parts.words: Some papers of James (according to North)
parts.note: Henry James's novella concerns the letters of a dead poet, sought by a scheming narrator

explanation.surface: Documents belonging to someone named James, as reported by someone named North.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry James's novella The Aspern Papers concerns the letters of the dead poet Jeffrey Aspern.

clue.text: Work of Camus carried by pet characters of Adams?

definitions.text: Work of Camus carried by pet characters of Adams?

parts.words: Work of Camus carried by pet characters of Adams?
parts.note: Richard Adams's novel about escaped laboratory dogs suspected of spreading disease shares its first words with Camus's novel

explanation.surface: Something by Camus held by Adams's animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Adams wrote 'The Plague Dogs', so the dogs carry Camus's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Camus's novel La Peste describes an epidemic in Oran; Adams's dogs are feared to be its carriers.

clue.text: Harris's mute creatures of Elias Entries submitted from

clue.text: To produce hot air describing costumes for Titus Andronicus?

parts.note: to gas is to talk idly at length, producing hot air

explanation.surface: Talking idly about the outfits for a Roman tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman citizens wore the toga, so a production of Shakespeare's Roman tragedy would dress its cast in them.

clue.text: A quarter of Vivaldi's most hackneyed offering

definitions.text: A quarter of Vivaldi's most hackneyed offering

parts.words: A quarter of Vivaldi's most hackneyed offering
parts.note: one of the four concertos of The Four Seasons, Vivaldi's most over-played work

explanation.surface: A slice of Vivaldi's best-worn piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The Four Seasons is in four concertos, one per season, so the fall concerto is a quarter of it.

clue.text: Character missing from Maria Edgeworth

definitions.meaning: a person who is not present
Edgeworth's 1812 novel about an Irish landlord living in London

explanation.surface: A figure who has gone from Edgeworth's pages.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone missing is away; Edgeworth's novel attacks landlords who left Irish estates to live in England.

clue.text: Pass by, like most of Vanbrugh's comedy

indicators.note: taking most of the title means dropping a letter, here its opening one

parts.note: Sir John Vanbrugh's Restoration comedy The Relapse

explanation.surface: Something that passes, like the greater part of a Restoration play.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that elapses goes by.

clue.text: Composer seems in a muddle (sees main problem)

indicators.note: letters in a muddle are jumbled, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A composer looks confused, seeing a big problem.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis 'sees main' is a second set of the same eight letters; 'problem' would be its anagram signal, a bonus parse.
explanation.definitionFit: Olivier Messiaen was a French twentieth-century composer, known for the Quartet for the End of Time.
